utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of those conversations, did you manage on any occasion to obtain clear information from him what was his area of responsibility or, rather, the area of responsibility of his unit?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Not specifically from him, no. No. My interpretation was he was the -- sort of the town commander in the immediate area around the Lasva Valley and out surrounding Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, you also learnt shortly, I believe from your introductory briefings already, that within the territory of Vitez municipality, which need not necessarily coincide with your understanding of regions or areas of responsibility, that there were various HVO units active in that municipality. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. There seemed to be other factions operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps learn anything in greater detail about their areas of responsibility in the first period of your stay?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I shall now like to ask you a couple of questions in connection with your meeting with Cerkez when you were accompanying the U.N. investigators. You recognised one of them on the photograph. Would you agree that that meeting took place on the 4th of May, the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember specific dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree that it was a short time after you had arrived and at the beginning of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had a witness here, one of the two investigators, who described in some detail -- he explicitly stated that present at that meeting was the investigator, Cerkez, Major Dundas-Whatley, an interpreter, an HVO security officer at the beginning of the meeting, and then halfway through the meeting Colonel Stewart joined in, but he never mentioned any other British officer being present in addition to Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm just coming to it, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the meeting in Cerkez's office that you attended together with you and investigators, was this person present that you showed us on the photograph, the one with the glasses, or was someone else present, the other person whose photograph you saw? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: There were two individuals. The one with the glasses, I remember he was one of the investigators. I can't remember who the other one was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were both present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. They were both conducting the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that meeting held in the cinema building, in Cerkez's office?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous statement you mentioned that nasty-looking man, armed to the teeth, who was present, and whose presence was rather unpleasant, and that he was there throughout the meeting. Are you sure that that person did not leave the room virtually before the meeting began?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No, I can't remember, but I do remember he was present. Whether he left through the meeting -- immediately before we got into the conversation, I can't remember, but I do remember him being in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try and remind you, refresh your memory. I know it was six years ago. Payam Akhavan said that he found the presence of this soldier unpleasant, and he asked Cerkez for the person to leave the meeting, and Cerkez did as he asked and the man left. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember. All I remember is he was there. Whether he stayed for the whole meeting or not, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said that it was Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen Darko Kraljevic before? Had you met him?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you then know that it was Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Because I remember the individual that was in the room, and then whether during the conversation with Mr. Cerkez or subsequently, I got to know this individual as Darko Kraljevic. I got to know his name. But it was definitely one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators, you said that he was dressed in black. If I show you that the witness told us that he was wearing a greyish-green sweater, a sweater worn by German troops, does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that he was wearing dark clothing. I don't know what you're referring to, Mr. Kovacic, as a witness wearing a greyish-green sweater. Is this another witness in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Payam Akhavan said this explicitly, and it seems to me there may have been two meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You see, you're asking the witness to comment on what another witness has said, and I don't know how useful that is. I rather doubt it's not very useful. You can certainly put to the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: fact, I will do so. Major Hay, was the witness or might the witness have been wearing -- might Kraljevic have been wearing a greyish-green sweater?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: He might well have been wearing a greyish-green sweater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let us round off that part. That individual whom you believed to be Darko Kraljevic attending the meeting, did he take part, any part, in the meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I don't think he did. I can't remember him taking part, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, did you take the floor at the meeting? Did you take an active part in the meeting or were you just an observer?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, it was the U.N. investigators. It was their shout basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember if your colleague Matthew Dundas-Whatley said something after the meeting when you left that place? Did he say anything about the manner in which Cerkez was interviewed by the U.N. representatives and defining it as cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I can't remember, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you remember if your colleague Major Dundas-Whatley showed that he was not very happy with the course of that meeting because he had a different idea about the maintenance of contact? Did he say anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Sorry, about the what? About the maintenance of contact? I'm sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My fault. I wasn't clear enough. As a liaison officer, you had the same role. Of course, you wanted to maintain with the local authorities, with local commanders, relations which would be the best possible, which would be the most correct possible so that you could continue keeping in touch with them and in contact with them. So that was in your best interest, wasn't that?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the meeting with Cerkez was over, did then your colleague Matthew Dundas-Whatley criticise in any way the tactic and the conduct of the U.N. investigators during the meeting with Cerkez; that is, that it was interfering with Matthew Dundas-Whatley's work?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I can't remember. He may well have done, but I'm sorry, I can't remember that specific event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you testified that you saw Darko Kraljevic on several other occasions in the vicinity or around Cerkez's headquarters, and I should like to remind you that in the statement which you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal in April 1997, on page 3, you say: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "Kraljevic together again after this meeting. Soon afterwards, I handed the Vitez area over to Captain Lee Whitworth." [Translation] So which of the two statements is true: what you told us today or what you said on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: What is true is I never saw Mario Cerkez and Dario Kordic together again. I saw, rather, Darko Kraljevic. Sorry. I saw Darko Kraljevic in and around the cinema and in the vicinity when I used to pop in to see Mario Cerkez, but I never actually saw them physically together again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're on the topic of Darko Kraljevic, let us close that part of the story with just one question more. A moment ago, when asked by my learned friend Sayers, answered that you learnt about the Vitezovi -- about the existence of the Vitezovi, of that particular HVO unit, much later, but did you associate it with Darko Kraljevic? Were you aware that he was the commander of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Not at that time particular time. Subsequently when this area had been handed over to Captain Whitworth, through the debriefs in the evenings, through the rest of the course of our time there, I got to associate with the name Vitezovi and Darko Kraljevic and the connotation between the two and just through talking to the other LOs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. During your tour of duty there and those briefings, did you learn anything about the origins of that unit of the Vitezovi, about its background, its history?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No. I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear ever anything about the existence of HOS units in Central Bosnia, H-O-S units?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of their existence as well. Again, after I had handed over the sort of Vitez area, that's when the HOS and the Vitezovi came to light, and I heard it through the grapevine, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you somehow learned that HOS units were more or less present in all the municipalities in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I knew of their existence. I didn't know their whereabouts, specific whereabouts, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to hear, to see, or read somewhere that at least until sometime in 1993, HOS units also included quite a number of Muslims and some of them were even commanding officers there?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No. I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just go back to that meeting with Cerkez. I have just one more question about that. You cannot recount to us in greater detail the conversation between Mr. Cerkez and the two investigators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the content of the conversation, no, I'm sorry, although it did sort of centralise around Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You referred to the convoy, and I do not want to go into that really, but I think there is just one question there. You mentioned women. You specifically mentioned women as active participants, as the actors of that incident when the convoy was stopped, but they were not HVO members; they were civilians. It was quite clear, wasn't that -- wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes. The convoy was stopped by women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, in view of the request you addressed to the present HVO soldiers, to stop those women and calm them down? So do you think that the army, the military, have any jurisdiction over these civilians, that they are called upon to introduce law and order and do anything with those civilians?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: They were present, they were armed, and given the nature of what was going on in the Lasva Valley at the time, I remember requesting them or beseeching them to sort of do something about it, and they wouldn't. They said they couldn't. As I said earlier on, I would argue the fact that they just wouldn't, not couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour in the Lasva Valley, Major, you could see that there was some civilian police, not only that it existed but that it was active; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: There were individuals or units on both sides who were appointed civilian police, but I would have different views as to actually who commanded them and who orchestrated their movements, et cetera. I would say they were controlled by the military at that time because there was complete breakdown in sort of infrastructure and everything. Everything was sort of commanded by the sort of military -- orchestrated by the military commanders around the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you arrived at this conclusion on the basis of all the information and everything that you learned during your tour there, is it?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: That's right. On my own sort of observations and experiences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a document or an incident from which it would clearly transpire that the civilian police was under the command of some undefined authority, political authority, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: It may well have been. I mean, when we arrived -- and I can't remember; I think it was in June -- there were a number of meetings going on with ECMM and ourselves, getting the heads of both sort of warring factions together, and there were a number of agreements, pacts, whatever you want to call it, that came out of it. But inevitably, as soon as it was signed, it was broken the next day anyway. That may be a cynical point of view, but it was also fact. So, really, I go back to the point that really, at that time, the military commanders -- "military commanders," inverted commas -- were the ones that sort of had the pool of everything at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we are now going some way from the evidence in chief, and the witness has given his evidence as to why he came to that conclusion. If you want to contradict it, of course, you can call evidence of your own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. Just one simple question on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same story, same convoy, and then we come to Nova Bila then, and the convoy was stopped again. And on that occasion, I think you said that you were there, and there were even two uniformed policemen; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I didn't specifically see the -- I didn't see the incident; I heard about it afterwards. But I heard the firing, and I was diverted away from the assisting to escort the convoy as I came across a gunshot-wound casualty, and I took that wounded individual in the back of my vehicle all the way back to Travnik, to the hospital in Travnik. And so I wasn't there on the ground for the rest of that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't remember the civilian policemen? Did you see them, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: As I said, I wasn't really involved in the rest of that incident, and I was evacuating a casualty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, about Grbavica, only a few questions, please. You mentioned that there was a sniper active in the area. Was that a sniper of the -- a BH army sniper? Was it from two houses, from two white houses, from the hollow or from the crest of the hill behind your camp?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes, I remember there was a Muslim sniper, from the house directly above what we called the officers' mess at the time, used to fire out of that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you ever informed that those two houses belonged to Serbs who had left the area, and so the snipers had taken them over as their base?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that that was not the only sniper in Grbavica, was it?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I'm sure there were others. I wasn't particularly aware of any -- any more, but it wouldn't surprise me to find out that there were more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, Grbavica was a point controlled by the BH army even before you arrived in the Lasva Valley, and I suppose you must have learned that at the briefings in your early days, and subsequently you also could see that?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is no doubt that that point commands the view of all the other points on all the slopes above the road, that practically it controls the principal route through the valley -- that is, the road between Travnik and Vitez -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So presumably you learnt and saw in no time that the HVO and civilians were compelled to use a roundabout route, which was not all that easy, if they wanted to move between Vitez and Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also learnt that on various occasions, people, either civilians or military, who would drive a vehicle and use that road in front of your camp -- that is, Grbavica -- in spite of the risk, that many of them fell victim to those snipers?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware, and I saw a number of individuals who were, unfortunately, shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the military operations ended and the HVO took over Grbavica and mopped up the area, the HVO -- the BH army withdrew from Grbavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, meanwhile, before the civilians, the refugees arrived, a team, a police team came, and it tried to investigate the tracks, the signs of the BH army's stay there, to collect weapons and see if there were any civilians left. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat that again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that that same evening when the fighting ended, on the 8th of September, in the late afternoon, to the village of Grbavica, a small civilian police team came in order to take stock of the situation and look for weapons and things like that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you recall that that night, a group of men, of civilians, looked for shelter there?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I remember a group of civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of all this, Mr. Kovacic? This witness simply saw the attack. You are asking him about a huge amount of background detail. I don't know that it's going to assist us to know about this. He said two things: One, that he saw the attack; he's agreed that it was a military target, but he said the destruction afterwards was too great. Now, that's all he said, and you have spent ten minutes or more asking him about a lot of detail that you can deal with in your own case. Now, have you any challenge to the specific evidence which he gave, which was that it was a military target -- presumably you don't dispute that -- or that the destruction was too great? Now, if you want to dispute that with the witness, you can; but we will be here for a very long time indeed if we go on like this, all this detail. The witness simply can't give detail about what the HVO did unless he was there. Now, could you concentrate your cross-examination, please, on those two matters, if you have any questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry if I did any mistake, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to apologise. It's not necessary. But the point is this, that can we concentrate in this case on evidence which the witness gives and can deal with? If you have a lot of other evidence about the background to it -- for instance, about how the civilians had to use a roundabout route -- the time to put that evidence forward is in your own case, rather than these endless arguments with each of the witnesses. Now, could we deal with the matters which the witness himself dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour, but could I then just tender a document which was earlier mentioned, and it refers to the situation in Grbavica after the military part of the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it deal with the destruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you say it's already been put into evidence, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the file, but without the number. If I can remind you, that was what I showed to Witness Whitworth, and he recognised his name and the contact. And then after we asked for the translation, I filed it; it is in the court file, but it is not marked as the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What is it? A milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is one report of the commander of uniformed police who was there on the site investigating the result of the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who is it an investigation by? Which police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The title is obvious from the stamp, and it has commander of uniformed police, part of police from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put the document to the witness. He may not be able to comment on it because he won't have seen it before, but you can put it to him, provided we do it briefly and then we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is Croatian text on the top, and the English and French is enclosed. And I can only ask the witness whether he recognises the name of his colleague, Captain Whitworth, who was mentioned by a police officer there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D43/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In order to speed out, last line in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you agree -- or do you know anything about it, that is -- that your colleague, Mr. Whitworth, was called Captain Perry by the HVO, and that he could react to this visit?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not slipping shoulders here, but the area of responsibility was Captain Whitworth's. I had no sort of jurisdiction in this area. I can't comment on this at all. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We heard in the evidence that he was referred to as Captain Perry; the witness himself told us that. This witness can't take the matter any further, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could that document be tendered as evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's been tendered. It's got a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, you personally, and your colleagues, often used terms such as Lasva Valley, the Vitez area, you used these descriptive terms, Novi Travnik/Vitez area; do those terms in any way coincide with the administrative territory of municipalities within the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I haven't a clue. I'm sorry. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for you, the administrative borders were not relevant, the borders of the municipalities, were they?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: For my day-to-day conduct of business, I split my area of responsibility, as it became then, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Turbe, and that was my sort of area of responsibility, my remit, basically. But I wasn't aware of any sort of administrative borders. If we were referring to any sort of borders, it was our interpretation of the sort of military structure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I think it is really time for you to limit yourself to a proper cross-examination. It is time for you to finish with it. You have taken a lot of time, in view of the content of the examination-in-chief, so will you please finish it off, if you have anything that is relevant, because all this has nothing to do with the witness, and please do so, so that we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that at Grbavica, the BH army forces had a stronghold south of Grbavica, on the other side of the road, across your camp, across your base?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: The BiH?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit Z2036, the photograph of the launcher for Bebes that you took, could you tell us -- roughly, of course -- where and when you took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly when; obviously during the summer of '93. But it was in the area of Bucici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vucici [sic], far from the town of Vitez, isn't it? I mean Vucici [sic], the place you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Bucici, just to the north-east of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember under whose control Bucici was, the HVO or the BiH?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: At the time, it was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that similar weapons and devices were used by both parties?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I believe so, but it was more -- more heavily used by the HVO, I think. That was my interpretation when I was out there. They were the ones who tended to use the improvised weapons more, as I found -- I think they had difficulty in getting sort of munitions and armaments at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another brief point: You said that in October '93, you visited the headquarters where Alagic was the commander of the 3rd Corps in Travnik, and that you saw there some 25 or 30 imprisoned HVO soldiers in the basement. The question is, did you have occasion to talk to any of those prisoners alone?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't request to speak to them alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about whether those prisoners were visited by the International Red Cross, whether they had any contact with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I can't specifically tell you if they had been visited by the time that I had seen them or visited immediately after, but I know that the ICRC were around the area at the time, conducting their own visits as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question in that connection: When Alagic showed you those prisoners, were you told whether they were newly arrested, a couple of days ago, or had some of them already spent several months there in detention?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told how long they had been there, but my interpretation was, from what I had seen of them, albeit that it would be very briefly, I didn't think they had been there for that long a -- that long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, perhaps, just one more question: Generally speaking, in the Lasva Valley, were both sides fighting to retain or gain control of the main roads running through the area?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: I can't really comment whether they were trying to gain control of the MSRs. Your Honour, if I'm going to answer this, it's going to -- I'm going to be here for another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you've been here long enough. Thank you. Look, Mr. Kovacic, we can have other evidence about this. No doubt we will hear from the armies themselves, who are the best people to answer it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was just looking to see whether a British officer could give us an overview. Could I just excuse myself for a minute to check whether I covered this. Just one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, in your statement I noticed the last line on page 5 you said: [In English] "I handed over a videotape to the investigator about this assault and immediate aftermath." That is in the part about Grbavica. [Interpretation] Did you ever hear or were you shown that video by the Prosecution? Do you know what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: The Prosecution have got it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I then take advantage of this opportunity to ask my learned friends across the aisle to give you a copy of that video, if they have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suspect you've seen it. We've seen a videotape of the Convoy of Joy. I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was about Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That video was not shown to the witness during the preparation for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has it been shown to the Defence? Have they got a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video and the witness can tell you exactly what it is. It's a compilation of stories, as far as I know, prepared by the BBC reporter, and which does not concern solely the attack on Grbavica. There are a variety of subjects which are very interesting, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what it concerns. It hasn't been played in the trial; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could check that out. We have had various videos. I don't remember one about Grbavica, but we've had some stills of Grbavica, and the Defence are probably entitled to receive the video in due course. Perhaps you would like to look into that, Mr. Lopez-Terres, and if there is any objection to handing it over, you can let us know. Otherwise, perhaps you might like to hand it over. Now, Mr. Kovacic, have you got anything more for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm done. [Interpretation] Thank you Major. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a point of clarification, should we communicate to the Defence only the part relating to the attack on Grbavica or everything that is contained in that video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, it's a matter for you to decide. If you have any doubt or difficulties about it, then you can refer the matter to us, but on the whole it's probably better to give them everything unless there's some good reason why you shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There's absolutely no reason, Mr. President. The totality of the videotape will be handed over. I have two small questions for the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hay, you were asked a moment ago whether you saw Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic at the HVO headquarters in Vitez, and you said, "no."

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we agree that after the beginning of June 1993, Vitez was no longer part of your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You no longer had occasion to go to the Vitez Hotel, did you?

utterances.speaker: Was it a greyish-green sweater?  And, in
utterances.text: Correct, and that's why I never saw them. If they did meet, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A second question concerning the deaths of the driver of the convoy of the UNHCR during an attack by the 7th Brigade. We agree, don't we, that the driver was not killed due to -- he was killed as a result of the unfortunate coincidence between the attack on the passing of the convoy?
